## A Dual Embedding Space Model for Document Ranking


---

arxiv_id: 1602.01137

version: 1

summary: A fundamental goal of search engines is to identify, given a query, documents that have relevant text. This is intrinsically difficult because the query and the document may use different vocabulary, or the document may contain query words without being relevant. We investigate neural word embeddings as a source of evidence in document ranking. We train a word2vec embedding model on a large unlabelled query corpus, but in contrast to how the model is commonly used, we retain both the input and the output projections, allowing us to leverage both the embedding spaces to derive richer distributional relationships. During ranking we map the query words into the input space and the document words into the output space, and compute a query-document relevance score by aggregating the cosine similarities across all the query-document word pairs.
  We postulate that the proposed Dual Embedding Space Model (DESM) captures evidence on whether a document is about a query term in addition to what is modelled by traditional term-frequency based approaches. Our experiments show that the DESM can re-rank top documents returned by a commercial Web search engine, like Bing, better than a term-matching based signal like TF-IDF. However, when ranking a larger set of candidate documents, we find the embeddings-based approach is prone to false positives, retrieving documents that are only loosely related to the query. We demonstrate that this problem can be solved effectively by ranking based on a linear mixture of the DESM and the word counting features.

## Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate


---

arxiv_id: 1409.0473

version: 7

summary: Neural machine translation is a recently proposed approach to machine translation. Unlike the traditional statistical machine translation, the neural machine translation aims at building a single neural network that can be jointly tuned to maximize the translation performance. The models proposed recently for neural machine translation often belong to a family of encoder-decoders and consists of an encoder that encodes a source sentence into a fixed-length vector from which a decoder generates a translation. In this paper, we conjecture that the use of a fixed-length vector is a bottleneck in improving the performance of this basic encoder-decoder architecture, and propose to extend this by allowing a model to automatically (soft-)search for parts of a source sentence that are relevant to predicting a target word, without having to form these parts as a hard segment explicitly. ## Learning Longer Memory in Recurrent Neural Networks


---

arxiv_id: 1412.7753

version: 2

summary: Recurrent neural network is a powerful model that learns temporal patterns in sequential data. For a long time, it was believed that recurrent networks are difficult to train using simple optimizers, such as stochastic gradient descent, due to the so-called vanishing gradient problem. In this paper, we show that learning longer term patterns in real data, such as in natural language, is perfectly possible using gradient descent. This is achieved by using a slight structural modification of the simple recurrent neural network architecture. We encourage some of the hidden units to change their state slowly by making part of the recurrent weight matrix close to identity, thus forming kind of a longer term memory. We evaluate our model in language modeling experiments, where we obtain similar performance to the much more complex Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) networks (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997).

## Noisy Activation Functions


---

arxiv_id: 1603.00391

version: 3

summary: Common nonlinear activation functions used in neural networks can cause training difficulties due to the saturation behavior of the activation function, which may hide dependencies that are not visible to vanilla-SGD (using first order gradients only). Gating mechanisms that use softly saturating activation functions to emulate the discrete switching of digital logic circuits are good examples of this. We propose to exploit the injection of appropriate noise so that the gradients may flow easily, even if the noiseless application of the activation function would yield zero gradient. Large noise will dominate the noise-free gradient and allow stochastic gradient descent toexplore more. By adding noise only to the problematic parts of the activation function, we allow the optimization procedure to explore the boundary between the degenerate (saturating) and the well-behaved parts of the activation function. We also establish connections to simulated annealing, when the amount of noise is annealed down, making it easier to optimize hard objective functions. We find experimentally that replacing such saturating activation functions by noisy variants helps training in many contexts, yielding state-of-the-art or competitive results on different datasets and task, especially when training seems to be the most difficult, e.g., when curriculum learning is necessary to obtain good results.

source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1603.00391v3

## Recurrent Highway Networks


---

arxiv_id: 1607.03474

version: 5

summary: Many sequential processing tasks require complex nonlinear transition functions from one step to the next. However, recurrent neural networks with 'deep' transition functions remain difficult to train, even when using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. We introduce a novel theoretical analysis of recurrent networks based on Gersgorin's circle theorem that illuminates several modeling and optimization issues and improves our understanding of the LSTM cell. Based on this analysis we propose Recurrent Highway Networks, which extend the LSTM architecture to allow step-to-step transition depths larger than one. Several language modeling experiments demonstrate that the proposed architecture results in powerful and efficient models. On the Penn Treebank corpus, solely increasing the transition depth from 1 to 10 improves word-level perplexity from 90.6 to 65.4 using the same number of parameters. On the larger Wikipedia datasets for character prediction (text8 and enwik8), RHNs outperform all previous results and achieve an entropy of 1.27 bits per character.

## Recurrent Highway Networks


---

arxiv_id: 1607.03474

version: 5

summary: Many sequential processing tasks require complex nonlinear transition functions from one step to the next. However, recurrent neural networks with 'deep' transition functions remain difficult to train, even when using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. We introduce a novel theoretical analysis of recurrent networks based on Gersgorin's circle theorem that illuminates several modeling and optimization issues and improves our understanding of the LSTM cell. Based on this analysis we propose Recurrent Highway Networks, which extend the LSTM architecture to allow step-to-step transition depths larger than one. Several language modeling experiments demonstrate that the proposed architecture results in powerful and efficient models. On the Penn Treebank corpus, solely increasing the transition depth from 1 to 10 improves word-level perplexity from 90.6 to 65.4 using the same number of parameters. On the larger Wikipedia datasets for character prediction (text8 and enwik8), RHNs outperform all previous results and achieve an entropy of 1.27 bits per character.

user_input: You have to use rag tool and retrieve at least one document: What is the mathematical definition of the Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) activation function?
response:
**The mathematical definition of the Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) activation function**, as introduced in the paper *Fast and Accurate Deep Network Learning by Exponential Linear Units (ELUs)* (Clevert et al., arXiv:1511.07289), is given by:

$$
f(x) =
\begin{cases}
x & \text{if } x > 0 \\
\alpha \left( e^{x} - 1 \right) & \text{if } x \leq 0
\end{cases}
$$

where \(\alpha > 0\) is a hyperparameter that controls the value to which the function saturates for negative inputs.

### Key Properties from the Paper
- For positive inputs, ELU behaves identically to the identity function (like ReLU), ensuring a derivative of 1 and avoiding the vanishing gradient problem.
- For negative inputs, ELU produces negative values that saturate to \(-\alpha\), pushing mean unit activations closer to zero. This reduces bias shift and brings the gradient closer to the natural gradient, accelerating learning.
- Unlike Leaky ReLUs or PReLUs, ELUs saturate to a negative value, providing a noise-robust deactivation state while decreasing forward-propagated variation.

The paper demonstrates that ELU networks achieve faster convergence and superior generalization compared to ReLU, LReLU, and SReLU on datasets such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, often outperforming ReLU networks even when the latter use batch normalization.

## Fast and Accurate Deep Network Learning by Exponential Linear Units (ELUs)


---

arxiv_id: 1511.07289

version: 5

summary: We introduce the "exponential linear unit" (ELU) which speeds up learning in deep neural networks and leads to higher classification accuracies. Like rectified linear units (ReLUs), leaky ReLUs (LReLUs) and parametrized ReLUs (PReLUs), ELUs alleviate the vanishing gradient problem via the identity for positive values. However, ELUs have improved learning characteristics compared to the units with other activation functions. In contrast to ReLUs, ELUs have negative values which allows them to push mean unit activations closer to zero like batch normalization but with lower computational complexity. Mean shifts toward zero speed up learning by bringing the normal gradient closer to the unit natural gradient because of a reduced bias shift effect. While LReLUs and PReLUs have negative values, too, they do not ensure a noise-robust deactivation state. ELUs saturate to a negative value with smaller inputs and thereby decrease the forward propagated variation and information. Therefore, ELUs code the degree of presence of particular phenomena in the input, while they do not quantitatively model the degree of their absence. In experiments, ELUs lead not only to faster learning, but also to significantly better generalization performance than ReLUs and LReLUs on networks with more than 5 layers. On CIFAR-100 ELUs networks significantly outperform ReLU networks with batch normalization while batch normalization does not improve ELU networks. ELU networks are among the top 10 reported CIFAR-10 results and yield the best published result on CIFAR-100, without resorting to multi-view evaluation or model averaging. On ImageNet, ELU networks considerably speed up learning compared to a ReLU network with the same architecture, obtaining less than 10% classification error for a single crop, single model network.

### Expected Technical Content (from the actual paper, for context)
In "Delving Deep into Rectifiers: Surpassing Human-Level Performance on ImageNet Classification" the authors derive a zero-mean Gaussian initialization for ReLU/PReLU layers that preserves variance of the forward signal:

Let \( n_l \) be the number of input connections (fan-in) to layer \( l \). The weight variance is set to
\[
\operatorname{Var}(W_l) = \frac{2}{n_l}.
\]
This ensures that if the input activations \( x \) to the layer satisfy \( \operatorname{Var}(x) = 1 \), the pre-activation variance after the linear transform and ReLU remains approximately 1:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(y) = n_l \cdot \operatorname{Var}(W) \cdot \operatorname{Var}(x) \approx 1,
\]
where the factor of 2 compensates for the fact that a ReLU zeros out roughly half the distribution (hence the "2" rather than "1" used in Xavier/Glorot initialization).

summary: Deeper neural networks are more difficult to train. We present a residual learning framework to ease the training of networks that are substantially deeper than those used previously. We explicitly reformulate the layers as learning residual functions with reference to the layer inputs, instead of learning unreferenced functions. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence showing that these residual networks are easier to optimize, and can gain accuracy from considerably increased depth. On the ImageNet dataset we evaluate residual nets with a depth of up to 152 layers---8x deeper than VGG nets but still having lower complexity. An ensemble of these residual nets achieves 3.57% error on the ImageNet test set. This result won the 1st place on the ILSVRC 2015 classification task. We also present analysis on CIFAR-10 with 100 and 1000 layers.
  The depth of representations is of central importance for many visual recognition tasks. Solely due to our extremely deep representations, we obtain a 28% relative improvement on the COCO object detection dataset. Deep residual nets are foundations of our submissions to ILSVRC & COCO 2015 competitions, where we also won the 1st places on the tasks of ImageNet detection, ImageNet localization, COCO detection, and COCO segmentation.

user_input: You have to use rag tool and retrieve at least one document: What mechanism does Monotonic Chunkwise Attention use to enable online, streamable sequence-to-sequence learning?
response:
**Monotonic Chunkwise Attention (MoChA)** enables **online, streamable sequence-to-sequence learning** through a **hybrid hard-monotonic + soft-chunkwise attention** mechanism (arXiv:1712.05382).

### Core Mechanism
MoChA combines two components:

1. **Hard monotonic attention** (inherited from Raffel et al., 2017)  
   - At each decoder timestep \(i\), the model scans the encoder memory \(h\) from left to right starting at position \(t_{i-1}\).  
   - It computes a **monotonic energy** \(e_{i,j} = \text{MonotonicEnergy}(s_{i-1}, h_j)\) and a selection probability \(p_{i,j} = \sigma(e_{i,j})\).  
   - The first position \(j\) where \(p_{i,j} \geq 0.5\) is chosen as the **stopping point** \(t_i = j\).  
   - This enforces **strict left-to-right monotonicity** and allows the decoder to emit an output symbol **without seeing future inputs**, enabling streaming/online decoding.

2. **Chunkwise soft attention**  
   - Instead of attending only to the single chosen memory entry \(h_{t_i}\), MoChA attends **softly over a fixed-size window of width \(w\)** ending at \(t_i\):  
     \[
     v = t_i - w + 1, \quad
     c_i = \sum_{k=v}^{t_i} \frac{\exp(u_{i,k})}{\sum_{m=v}^{t_i} \exp(u_{i,m})} \, h_k
     \]
     where \(u_{i,k} = \text{ChunkEnergy}(s_{i-1}, h_k)\) is a separate energy function.  
   - The context vector \(c_i\) is thus a **weighted average over the chunk** \([v, t_i]\), providing limited local reordering and softness while preserving monotonicity of chunk placement.

### Online / Streamable Properties
- **Linear-time decoding**: The monotonic scan never revisits earlier positions; each output step continues from \(t_{i-1}\).
- **Constant-factor overhead**: Complexity is \(O(T + w)\) per output step (vs. \(O(T^2)\) for standard soft attention).
- **Training**: Uses the expected context vector \(\mathbb{E}[c_i]\) computed via an efficient parallel formulation involving moving sums over the monotonic probabilities \(\alpha_{i,:}\) and chunk softmaxes, allowing standard backpropagation.

**Key equations** (from the paper):
- Monotonic probability: \(\alpha_{i,j} = p_{i,j} \prod_{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - p_{i,k})\)
- Chunkwise distribution: \(\beta_{i,j}\) obtained via moving-sum normalization over windows of size \(w\)
- Context: \(c_i = \sum_j \beta_{i,j} h_j\)

When \(w=1\), MoChA reduces exactly to hard monotonic attention. Larger \(w\) (typically small, e.g., 2–4) recovers much of the expressivity of soft attention while retaining online capability.

This design is what allows MoChA to match offline soft-attention performance on speech recognition (WER) and significantly outperform pure monotonic attention on summarization, all while supporting real-time streaming inference.

summary: Sequence-to-sequence models with soft attention have been successfully applied to a wide variety of problems, but their decoding process incurs a quadratic time and space cost and is inapplicable to real-time sequence transduction. user_input: You have to use rag tool and retrieve at least one document: How do HyperNetworks compute the weights of another target network dynamically?
response:
**HyperNetworks** (Ha et al., arXiv:1609.09106) compute the weights of a **target network** (the "phenotype") dynamically by using a smaller auxiliary network (the **hypernetwork**, or "genotype") that takes an embedding or conditioning vector as input and directly outputs the parameters of the target.

## Static Case (e.g., Convolutional Networks)
A hypernetwork \(H\) receives a **layer embedding** \(z_l \in \mathbb{R}^{N_z}\) for each layer \(l\) and produces the full weight tensor of that layer:
\[
W_l = H(z_l) \quad \text{or more generally} \quad W_l = f\bigl(d(z_l)\bigr)
\]
where \(d(z_l)\) is an intermediate projection and \(f\) reshapes or linearly combines basis matrices.

- The same hypernetwork is reused across layers, enforcing a relaxed form of weight-sharing.
- Because \(z_l\) differs per layer, the generated weights \(W_l\) are **non-shared** while the total parameter count remains low (the hypernetwork itself is small).

## Dynamic Case (HyperRNN / HyperLSTM)
For recurrent networks the hypernetwork becomes **time-dependent**. At every timestep \(t\):

1. The hypernetwork (itself an RNN) receives the concatenation \([x_t; h_{t-1}]\) and produces a hidden state \(\hat{h}_t\).
2. Linear projections of \(\hat{h}_t\) yield low-dimensional **embeddings**:
   \[
   z_h,\; z_x,\; z_b = \text{linear}(\hat{h}_t)
   \]
3. These embeddings modulate the target RNN’s weight matrices via a **row-wise scaling** (memory-efficient formulation):
   \[
   W(z) = W_0 \odot d(z) \qquad \text{(element-wise scaling of each row)}
   \]
   or, equivalently,
   \[
   W_h(t) = W_h \cdot \text{diag}\bigl(d(z_h)\bigr),\quad
   W_x(t) = W_x \cdot \text{diag}\bigl(d(z_x)\bigr).
   \]
4. The target RNN then performs its update with the newly generated, timestep-specific weights:
   \[
   h_t = \phi\bigl(W_h(t)\,h_{t-1} + W_x(t)\,x_t + b(t)\bigr).
   \]

Both networks are trained **end-to-end** with back-propagation; gradients flow through the hypernetwork into the generated weights and back to the hypernetwork parameters.

## Key Properties
- **Dynamic weight generation** occurs because the conditioning vector (\(z_l\) or \(\hat{h}_t\)) changes at every layer or timestep.
- The approach trades full expressivity for drastic parameter reduction: instead of storing \(N_z\) full matrices, only a scaling vector of size \(N_h\) (hidden size) is needed per step.
- This yields a **relaxed weight-sharing** regime—weights are neither completely tied across time/layers nor completely independent.

Thus HyperNetworks realize dynamic, input- or layer-conditioned parameter synthesis for a target network while remaining fully differentiable and scalable.

---

arxiv_id: 1609.09106

version: 4

summary: This work explores hypernetworks: an approach of using a one network, also known as a hypernetwork, to generate the weights for another network. Hypernetworks provide an abstraction that is similar to what is found in nature: the relationship between a genotype - the hypernetwork - and a phenotype - the main network. Though they are also reminiscent of HyperNEAT in evolution, our hypernetworks are trained end-to-end with backpropagation and thus are usually faster. The focus of this work is to make hypernetworks useful for deep convolutional networks and long recurrent networks, where hypernetworks can be viewed as relaxed form of weight-sharing across layers. Our main result is that hypernetworks can generate non-shared weights for LSTM and achieve near state-of-the-art results on a variety of sequence modelling tasks including character-level language modelling, handwriting generation and neural machine translation, challenging the weight-sharing paradigm for recurrent networks. Our results also show that hypernetworks applied to convolutional networks still achieve respectable results for image recognition tasks compared to state-of-the-art baseline models while requiring fewer learnable parameters.

## Decoupled Neural Interfaces using Synthetic Gradients


---

arxiv_id: 1608.05343

version: 2

summary: Training directed neural networks typically requires forward-propagating data through a computation graph, followed by backpropagating error signal, to produce weight updates. All layers, or more generally, modules, of the network are therefore locked, in the sense that they must wait for the remainder of the network to execute forwards and propagate error backwards before they can be updated. In this work we break this constraint by decoupling modules by introducing a model of the future computation of the network graph. These models predict what the result of the modelled subgraph will produce using only local information. In particular we focus on modelling error gradients: by using the modelled synthetic gradient in place of true backpropagated error gradients we decouple subgraphs, and can update them independently and asynchronously i.e. we realise decoupled neural interfaces. We show results for feed-forward models, where every layer is trained asynchronously, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) where predicting one's future gradient extends the time over which the RNN can effectively model, and also a hierarchical RNN system with ticking at different timescales. Finally, we demonstrate that in addition to predicting gradients, the same framework can be used to predict inputs, resulting in models which are decoupled in both the forward and backwards pass -- amounting to independent networks which co-learn such that they can be composed into a single functioning corporation.

## Fast and Accurate Deep Network Learning by Exponential Linear Units (ELUs)


---

arxiv_id: 1511.07289

version: 5

summary: We introduce the "exponential linear unit" (ELU) which speeds up learning in deep neural networks and leads to higher classification accuracies. Like rectified linear units (ReLUs), leaky ReLUs (LReLUs) and parametrized ReLUs (PReLUs), ELUs alleviate the vanishing gradient problem via the identity for positive values. However, ELUs have improved learning characteristics compared to the units with other activation functions. In contrast to ReLUs, ELUs have negative values which allows them to push mean unit activations closer to zero like batch normalization but with lower computational complexity. Mean shifts toward zero speed up learning by bringing the normal gradient closer to the unit natural gradient because of a reduced bias shift effect. While LReLUs and PReLUs have negative values, too, they do not ensure a noise-robust deactivation state. ELUs saturate to a negative value with smaller inputs and thereby decrease the forward propagated variation and information. Therefore, ELUs code the degree of presence of particular phenomena in the input, while they do not quantitatively model the degree of their absence. In experiments, ELUs lead not only to faster learning, but also to significantly better generalization performance than ReLUs and LReLUs on networks with more than 5 layers. On CIFAR-100 ELUs networks significantly outperform ReLU networks with batch normalization while batch normalization does not improve ELU networks. ELU networks are among the top 10 reported CIFAR-10 results and yield the best published result on CIFAR-100, without resorting to multi-view evaluation or model averaging. On ImageNet, ELU networks considerably speed up learning compared to a ReLU network with the same architecture, obtaining less than 10% classification error for a single crop, single model network.

## Layer Normalization


---

arxiv_id: 1607.06450

version: 1

summary: Training state-of-the-art, deep neural networks is computationally expensive. One way to reduce the training time is to normalize the activities of the neurons. A recently introduced technique called batch normalization uses the distribution of the summed input to a neuron over a mini-batch of training cases to compute a mean and variance which are then used to normalize the summed input to that neuron on each training case. This significantly reduces the training time in feed-forward neural networks. However, the effect of batch normalization is dependent on the mini-batch size and it is not obvious how to apply it to recurrent neural networks. In this paper, we transpose batch normalization into layer normalization by computing the mean and variance used for normalization from all of the summed inputs to the neurons in a layer on a single training case. Like batch normalization, we also give each neuron its own adaptive bias and gain which are applied after the normalization but before the non-linearity. Unlike batch normalization, layer normalization performs exactly the same computation at training and test times. It is also straightforward to apply to recurrent neural networks by computing the normalization statistics separately at each time step. Layer normalization is very effective at stabilizing the hidden state dynamics in recurrent networks. Empirically, we show that layer normalization can substantially reduce the training time compared with previously published techniques.

## Regularization and nonlinearities for neural language models: when are they needed?


---

arxiv_id: 1301.5650

version: 2

summary: Neural language models (LMs) based on recurrent neural networks (RNN) are some of the most successful word and character-level LMs. Why do they work so well, in particular better than linear neural LMs? Possible explanations are that RNNs have an implicitly better regularization or that RNNs have a higher capacity for storing patterns due to their nonlinearities or both. Here we argue for the first explanation in the limit of little training data and the second explanation for large amounts of text data. We show state-of-the-art performance on the popular and small Penn dataset when RNN LMs are regularized with random dropout. Nonetheless, we show even better performance from a simplified, much less expressive linear RNN model without off-diagonal entries in the recurrent matrix. We call this model an impulse-response LM (IRLM). Using random dropout, column normalization and annealed learning rates, IRLMs develop neurons that keep a memory of up to 50 words in the past and achieve a perplexity of 102.5 on the Penn dataset. On two large datasets however, the same regularization methods are unsuccessful for both models and the RNN's expressivity allows it to overtake the IRLM by 10 and 20 percent perplexity, respectively. Despite the perplexity gap, IRLMs still outperform RNNs on the Microsoft Research Sentence Completion (MRSC) task. We develop a slightly modified IRLM that separates long-context units (LCUs) from short-context units and show that the LCUs alone achieve a state-of-the-art performance on the MRSC task of 60.8%. Our analysis indicates that a fruitful direction of research for neural LMs lies in developing more accessible internal representations, and suggests an optimization regime of very high momentum terms for effectively training such models.

user_input: You have to use rag tool and retrieve at least one document: How does the Maxout activation function generalize both ReLU and Leaky ReLU?
response:
**Maxout** generalizes both **ReLU** and **Leaky ReLU** by replacing a fixed piecewise-linear activation with a *learned* piecewise-linear convex function obtained via max-pooling over *k* affine transformations.

### 1. Formal Definition (from Goodfellow et al., arXiv:1302.4389)

A maxout hidden layer computes
\[
h_i(\mathbf{x}) = \max_{j\in\{1,\dots,k\}} \bigl(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{W}_{:,:,i,j} + b_{i,j}\bigr)
\]
where \(\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m\times k}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}\).  
Each output unit therefore selects the *maximum* response among *k* linear “feature detectors.”

### 2. Special Cases that Recover ReLU and Leaky ReLU

- **ReLU** (\(k=2\))  
  Fix one of the two linear maps to be the zero function:
  \[
  \mathbf{W}_{:,:,i,2}=\mathbf{0},\quad b_{i,2}=0.
  \]
  Then
  \[
  h_i(\mathbf{x})=\max\bigl(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{W}_{:,:,i,1}+b_{i,1},\;0\bigr)
  \]
  which is exactly the standard ReLU.

- **Leaky ReLU** (\(k=2\))  
  Let the second map be a scaled copy of the first with a small negative slope \(\alpha>0\):
  \[
  \mathbf{W}_{:,:,i,2}=\alpha\mathbf{W}_{:,:,i,1},\quad b_{i,2}=\alpha b_{i,1}.
  \]
  Then
  \[
  h_i(\mathbf{x})=\max\bigl(z_i,\;\alpha z_i\bigr)
  \]
  where \(z_i=\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{W}_{:,:,i,1}+b_{i,1}\).  
  This yields the classic Leaky ReLU (or PReLU when \(\alpha\) is learned).

Thus any network that can be expressed with ReLU or Leaky ReLU is a *strict special case* of a maxout network with *k=2* and appropriately constrained weights.

### 3. Why This Is a True Generalization

- **Piecewise linearity & convexity**: Maxout remains piecewise linear and convex (the pointwise maximum of linear functions), preserving the optimization-friendly properties of ReLU.
- **Learned activation shape**: Instead of hand-designing the negative slope (as in Leaky ReLU) or forcing it to zero (ReLU), the network *learns* which of the *k* linear pieces is active for each input region.
- **Subspace pooling interpretation** (Springenberg & Riedmiller, arXiv:1312.6116): each maxout unit pools over a *k*-dimensional linear subspace, giving a tunable degree of invariance that ReLU (a 1-dimensional half-space) cannot achieve.

### 4. Empirical Support from Retrieved Papers

- Goodfellow et al. (arXiv:1302.4389) explicitly state: “A single maxout unit can be interpreted as making a piecewise linear approximation to an arbitrary convex function.”
- Springenberg & Riedmiller (arXiv:1312.6116) emphasize that maxout “can be seen as a generalization of rectified linear units (ReLUs)” while preserving dropout compatibility and gradient flow.
- Agostinelli et al. (arXiv:1412.6830) note that learned APL units often *resemble* Leaky ReLUs, reinforcing that maxout’s extra degrees of freedom subsume these fixed-slope variants.

In short, **Maxout** recovers both ReLU and Leaky ReLU by constraining two of its linear maps, yet offers a strictly richer family of activations when *k>2* or when all *k* maps are free parameters.

summary: We present a probabilistic variant of the recently introduced maxout unit. The success of deep neural networks utilizing maxout can partly be attributed to favorable performance under dropout, when compared to rectified linear units. It however also depends on the fact that each maxout unit performs a pooling operation over a group of linear transformations and is thus partially invariant to changes in its input. Starting from this observation we ask the question: Can the desirable properties of maxout units be preserved while improving their invariance properties ? summary: We propose a novel deep network structure called "Network In Network" (NIN) to enhance model discriminability for local patches within the receptive field. The conventional convolutional layer uses linear filters followed by a nonlinear activation function to scan the input. Instead, we build micro neural networks with more complex structures to abstract the data within the receptive field. We instantiate the micro neural network with a multilayer perceptron, which is a potent function approximator. The feature maps are obtained by sliding the micro networks over the input in a similar manner as CNN; they are then fed into the next layer. Deep NIN can be implemented by stacking mutiple of the above described structure. With enhanced local modeling via the micro network, we are able to utilize global average pooling over feature maps in the classification layer, which is easier to interpret and less prone to overfitting than traditional fully connected layers. We demonstrated the state-of-the-art classification performances with NIN on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and reasonable performances on SVHN and MNIST datasets.

summary: When a large feedforward neural network is trained on a small training set, it typically performs poorly on held-out test data. This "overfitting" is greatly reduced by randomly omitting half of the feature detectors on each training case. This prevents complex co-adaptations in which a feature detector is only helpful in the context of several other specific feature detectors. Instead, each neuron learns to detect a feature that is generally helpful for producing the correct answer given the combinatorially large variety of internal contexts in which it must operate. Random "dropout" gives big improvements on many benchmark tasks and sets new records for speech and object recognition.

summary: We propose a novel deep network structure called "Network In Network" (NIN) to enhance model discriminability for local patches within the receptive field. The conventional convolutional layer uses linear filters followed by a nonlinear activation function to scan the input. Instead, we build micro neural networks with more complex structures to abstract the data within the receptive field. We instantiate the micro neural network with a multilayer perceptron, which is a potent function approximator. The feature maps are obtained by sliding the micro networks over the input in a similar manner as CNN; they are then fed into the next layer. Deep NIN can be implemented by stacking mutiple of the above described structure. With enhanced local modeling via the micro network, we are able to utilize global average pooling over feature maps in the classification layer, which is easier to interpret and less prone to overfitting than traditional fully connected layers. We demonstrated the state-of-the-art classification performances with NIN on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and reasonable performances on SVHN and MNIST datasets.

response:
**Core architectural difference** between **Highway Networks** (Srivastava et al., 2015) and **Deep Residual Networks** (He et al., 2015):

## Highway Networks
The defining mechanism is **learned, data-dependent gating** via two parametric gates:

- **Transform gate**: \( T(x) = \sigma(W_T x + b_T) \)
- **Carry gate**: \( C(x) = 1 - T(x) \) (or independently parameterized)

The layer output is formed as:
\[
y = H(x, W_H) \odot T(x) + x \odot C(x)
\]
where \( H(\cdot) \) is a non-linear transformation (typically with ReLU or tanh).

- The gates are **learned parameters** and can completely “close” the shortcut (when \( T(x) \to 0 \)), effectively turning the block into a conventional layer.
- This gives the network explicit control over information flow, allowing “information highways” across many layers.

## Deep Residual Networks (ResNet)
The defining mechanism is a **fixed, parameter-free identity shortcut**:

\[
y = F(x, W_F) + x
\]

- The shortcut connection is **always open**; the residual function \( F \) is added to the identity.
- No learned gating is applied to the skip path; the formulation forces every block to learn a **residual function** relative to its input.

## Key Contrast (from the source papers)

| Aspect                    | Highway Networks                          | ResNet                                      |
|---------------------------|-------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Shortcut type             | Gated (parametric, data-dependent)        | Identity (fixed, parameter-free)            |
| Gate parameters           | Yes (\( T, C \))                          | None                                        |
| Behavior when “closed”    | Can become non-residual                   | Always residual                             |
| Information flow control  | Learned regulation                        | Unconditional pass-through                  |
| Demonstrated extreme depth| Hundreds of layers                        | Thousands of layers (with identity mapping) |

**Summary**: Highway Networks introduce **learnable transform/carry gates** that dynamically regulate the shortcut, whereas ResNet replaces gating with a **static identity mapping**, guaranteeing that every layer learns a residual function. This distinction is explicitly stated in the ResNet paper (arXiv:1512.03385) when contrasting the two architectures.

version: 1

summary: Rectified activation units (rectifiers) are essential for state-of-the-art neural networks. In this work, we study rectifier neural networks for image classification from two aspects. First, we propose a Parametric Rectified Linear Unit (PReLU) that generalizes the traditional rectified unit. PReLU improves model fitting with nearly zero extra computational cost and little overfitting risk. Second, we derive a robust initialization method that particularly considers the rectifier nonlinearities. This method enables us to train extremely deep rectified models directly from scratch and to investigate deeper or wider network architectures. Based on our PReLU networks (PReLU-nets), we achieve 4.94% top-5 test error on the ImageNet 2012 classification dataset. This is a 26% relative improvement over the ILSVRC 2014 winner (GoogLeNet, 6.66%). To our knowledge, our result is the first to surpass human-level performance (5.1%, Russakovsky et al.) on this visual recognition challenge.

user_input: You have to use rag tool and retrieve at least one document: How does the Factorization trick reduce parameters in LSTM networks without a significant loss of accuracy?
response:
**Answer based on the retrieved paper (arXiv:1703.10722) "Factorization tricks for LSTM networks" by Kuchaiev & Ginsburg.**

## Factorized LSTM (F-LSTM) Cell

The **factorization trick** (called *matrix factorization by design*) approximates the large weight matrix \(W\) of an LSTMP cell as the product of two smaller matrices:

\[
W \approx W_2 \cdot W_1
\]

where:
- \(W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{2p \times r}\)
- \(W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times 4n}\)
- \(r < p \leq n\) is the chosen **rank** (bottleneck dimension)

### Parameter Reduction Formula

**Original LSTMP parameters** (single matrix):
\[
|W| = 2p \times 4n
\]

**Factorized parameters**:
\[
|W_1| + |W_2| = (2p \cdot r) + (r \cdot 4n) = r(2p + 4n)
\]

**Savings**:
\[
\Delta = 2p \cdot 4n - r(2p + 4n) = (2p \cdot 4n) - r(2p + 4n)
\]

When \(r \ll 2p, 4n\), the reduction is substantial (often 2–3× fewer RNN parameters).

## Why Accuracy Is Preserved

- The method relies on the empirical observation that the full-rank matrix \(W\) can be **well-approximated by a low-rank matrix** of rank \(r\).
- The network is trained end-to-end with the factorization built into the architecture, allowing the optimizer to learn the most useful low-rank factors rather than post-hoc compression.
- On the **One Billion Word Benchmark**, the F-LSTM model achieved **perplexity 36.3** vs. the baseline BIGLSTM perplexity of **35.1**, while using **2–3× fewer RNN parameters**.

## Comparison with the Group LSTM (G-LSTM) Variant

The same paper also introduces **G-LSTM** (group partitioning), which splits inputs/hidden states into \(k\) independent groups. While both methods reduce parameters, the factorization approach is a direct low-rank matrix approximation, whereas grouping enforces block-diagonal structure.

### Summary Table (from paper results)

| Model       | RNN Parameters | Perplexity (1B Word) | Training Speed |
|-------------|----------------|----------------------|----------------|
| BIGLSTM     | baseline       | 35.1                 | baseline       |
| F-LSTM      | 2–3× fewer     | 36.3                 | faster         |
| G-LSTM      | 2–3× fewer     | 36.0                 | faster         |

**Key takeaway**: By enforcing a low-rank factorization \(W \approx W_2 W_1\) directly in the LSTM cell design, the model dramatically cuts parameters with only marginal perplexity degradation, because the essential information in the original weight matrix lies in a much lower-dimensional subspace.

arxiv_id: 1701.06538

version: 1

summary: The capacity of a neural network to absorb information is limited by its number of parameters. Conditional computation, where parts of the network are active on a per-example basis, has been proposed in theory as a way of dramatically increasing model capacity without a proportional increase in computation. In practice, however, there are significant algorithmic and performance challenges. In this work, we address these challenges and finally realize the promise of conditional computation, achieving greater than 1000x improvements in model capacity with only minor losses in computational efficiency on modern GPU clusters. We introduce a Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts layer (MoE), consisting of up to thousands of feed-forward sub-networks. A trainable gating network determines a sparse combination of these experts to use for each example. We apply the MoE to the tasks of language modeling and machine translation, where model capacity is critical for absorbing the vast quantities of knowledge available in the training corpora. We present model architectures in which a MoE with up to 137 billion parameters is applied convolutionally between stacked LSTM layers. On large language modeling and machine translation benchmarks, these models achieve significantly better results than state-of-the-art at lower computational cost.

## Google's Neural Machine Translation System: Bridging the Gap between Human and Machine Translation


---

arxiv_id: 1609.08144

version: 2

summary: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) is an end-to-end learning approach for automated translation, with the potential to overcome many of the weaknesses of conventional phrase-based translation systems. Unfortunately, NMT systems are known to be computationally expensive both in training and in translation inference. Also, most NMT systems have difficulty with rare words. These issues have hindered NMT's use in practical deployments and services, where both accuracy and speed are essential. In this work, we present GNMT, Google's Neural Machine Translation system, which attempts to address many of these issues. Our model consists of a deep LSTM network with 8 encoder and 8 decoder layers using attention and residual connections. To improve parallelism and therefore decrease training time, our attention mechanism connects the bottom layer of the decoder to the top layer of the encoder. To accelerate the final translation speed, we employ low-precision arithmetic during inference computations. To improve handling of rare words, we divide words into a limited set of common sub-word units ("wordpieces") for both input and output. This method provides a good balance between the flexibility of "character"-delimited models and the efficiency of "word"-delimited models, naturally handles translation of rare words, and ultimately improves the overall accuracy of the system. Our beam search technique employs a length-normalization procedure and uses a coverage penalty, which encourages generation of an output sentence that is most likely to cover all the words in the source sentence. On the WMT'14 English-to-French and English-to-German benchmarks, GNMT achieves competitive results to state-of-the-art. Using a human side-by-side evaluation on a set of isolated simple sentences, it reduces translation errors by an average of 60% compared to Google's phrase-based production system.

**Depth-Gated LSTM (DGLSTM) Architecture**

The **Depth-Gated LSTM** (arXiv:1508.03790) extends the standard stacked LSTM by introducing a **depth gate** that creates a *gated linear dependence* between memory cells of adjacent layers. This allows controlled memory flow vertically through the network depth, mitigating vanishing/exploding gradients when stacking recurrent layers.

### Standard LSTM Recap (for Context)
In a conventional LSTM at layer \(L\) and time \(t\):
- Memory cell: \(c_t^{(L)}\)
- Gates: input \(i_t^{(L)}\), forget \(f_t^{(L)}\), output \(o_t^{(L)}\)
- Candidate cell: \(\tilde{c}_t^{(L)} = \tanh(W_c x_t^{(L)} + U_c h_{t-1}^{(L)})\)
- Cell update: \(c_t^{(L)} = f_t^{(L)} \odot c_{t-1}^{(L)} + i_t^{(L)} \odot \tilde{c}_t^{(L)}\)
- Hidden state: \(h_t^{(L)} = o_t^{(L)} \odot \tanh(c_t^{(L)})\)

### Depth-Gated Extension
DGLSTM modifies the **memory cell computation** at layer \(L+1\) to include a linear contribution from the layer below (\(L\)) modulated by a learned depth gate \(d_t^{(L+1)}\).

The key equations are:

1. **Depth gate** (new component):
   \[
   d_t^{(L+1)} = \sigma\left(W_d^{(L+1)} c_t^{(L)} + U_d^{(L+1)} h_{t-1}^{(L+1)} + V_d^{(L+1)} c_{t-1}^{(L+1)}\right)
   \]
   where \(\sigma\) is the sigmoid function. The gate depends on:
   - The **lower-layer memory cell** \(c_t^{(L)}\)
   - The **previous hidden state** of the current layer \(h_{t-1}^{(L+1)}\)
   - The **previous memory cell** of the current layer \(c_{t-1}^{(L+1)}\)

2. **Memory cell update** (modified):
   \[
   c_t^{(L+1)} = f_t^{(L+1)} \odot c_{t-1}^{(L+1)} + i_t^{(L+1)} \odot \tilde{c}_t^{(L+1)} + d_t^{(L+1)} \odot c_t^{(L)}
   \]
   - The first two terms are the standard LSTM temporal recurrence.
   - The third term \(d_t^{(L+1)} \odot c_t^{(L)}\) injects a **gated linear copy** of the lower layer’s memory cell.

3. **Optional first-layer connection** (\(L=0\)):
   The same mechanism can connect the input features \(x_t^{(0)}\) directly to the first-layer memory cell via a depth gate.

### How Depth Gating Controls Memory Flow

- **Gated Linear Pathway**: Instead of forcing information through multiple non-linear transformations when moving up layers, DGLSTM provides a direct (but gated) linear path between memory cells. This is analogous to residual or highway connections but applied specifically to the *memory state*.
- **Selective Propagation**: The sigmoid depth gate \(d_t^{(L+1)}\) learns to regulate *how much* of the lower layer’s memory content should be copied upward at each time step. Values near 0 block flow; values near 1 allow full linear transfer.
- **Gradient Flow**: Because the connection is linear (scaled by \(d_t^{(L+1)}\)), gradients can back-propagate directly from upper layers to lower-layer memory cells without repeated non-linear squashing, alleviating vanishing gradients across depth.
- **Temporal + Depth Recurrence**: The architecture maintains the standard LSTM temporal gating (\(f_t, i_t\)) while adding an orthogonal depth-wise gating dimension.

### Relation to Similar Architectures (from Paper)
- **Highway Networks**: Share the gated linear bypass idea, but DGLSTM applies it to memory cells rather than layer outputs and retains the original LSTM input/output gates.
- **Grid LSTM**: A more general case; DGLSTM is essentially Grid LSTM restricted to time and depth dimensions on memory cells only.

**Empirical Results** (from the paper):
- Penn Treebank language modeling: DGLSTM achieved **96** perplexity vs. 117 for standard LSTM.
- Machine translation (BTEC): Improved BLEU scores.

This design enables deeper recurrent stacks while preserving the long-term memory properties of LSTMs through controlled vertical memory flow.

arxiv_id: 1508.03790

summary: In this short note, we present an extension of long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks to using a depth gate to connect memory cells of adjacent layers. Doing so introduces a linear dependence between lower and upper layer recurrent units. Importantly, the linear dependence is gated through a gating function, which we call depth gate. This gate is a function of the lower layer memory cell, the input to and the past memory cell of this layer. response:
**Neural SDE stabilizes Neural ODE by augmenting its deterministic dynamics with a stochastic diffusion term, effectively injecting continuous-time noise (modeling dropout, Gaussian noise, etc.) that regularizes trajectories and improves robustness.**

### Neural ODE Baseline (Deterministic Dynamics)
The standard **Neural ODE** evolves hidden states via the deterministic ODE:
\[
\frac{dh_t}{dt} = f(h_t, t; w)
\]
where \(f\) is a neural network (the “drift”). This is a continuous-depth analogue of a ResNet residual block. However, being fully deterministic, it lacks the regularization mechanisms (dropout, additive/multiplicative noise) common in discrete networks, leading to overfitting and sensitivity to input perturbations.

### Neural SDE Formulation (Stochastic Stabilization)
**Neural SDE** (Liu et al., arXiv:1906.02355) replaces the above with an Itô SDE:
\[
dh_t = f(h_t, t; w)\,dt + G(h_t, t; v)\,dB_t
\]
- \(f(\cdot)\) remains the neural drift (same as Neural ODE).
- \(G(\cdot)\) is a parameterized diffusion matrix (can realize Bernoulli/dropout noise, additive or multiplicative Gaussian noise).
- \(B_t\) is an \(m\)-dimensional Brownian motion.

The diffusion term \(G\,dB_t\) continuously perturbs trajectories, acting as a drop-in stochastic regularizer.

### Mechanism of Stabilization via Stochastic Noise
A 1-D toy example illustrates the effect (paper, §4):

- **Pure ODE** (\(\sigma=0\)): \(dx_t = x_t\,dt\) yields \(x_t = c_0 e^t\). Any nonzero \(c_0\) diverges exponentially; small perturbations are amplified.
- **SDE** (\(\sigma > 1\)): \(dx_t = x_t\,dt + \sigma x_t\,dB_t\) yields the explicit solution
  \[
  x_t = c_0 \exp\!\Bigl((1-\tfrac12\sigma^2)t + \sigma B_t\Bigr) \quad\text{a.s.}
  \]
  The extra \(-\frac12\sigma^2\) drift correction plus the martingale term \(\sigma B_t\) keep paths bounded on average, demonstrating that sufficient noise prevents divergence.

In the multi-dimensional case the same principle holds: the stochastic integral damps unstable modes that would otherwise explode under the deterministic flow.

### Theoretical Robustness Analysis (Stability of Perturbations)
Consider two nearby initial conditions \(h_0\) and \(\tilde h_0 = h_0 + \varepsilon_0\) (\(\|\varepsilon_0\|\le\delta\)). Their difference \(\varepsilon_t = \tilde h_t - h_t\) obeys the variational SDE (paper, Eq. 12):
\[
d\varepsilon_t = \bigl[f(\tilde h_t,t;w)-f(h_t,t;w)\bigr]dt + \bigl[G(\tilde h_t,t;v)-G(h_t,t;v)\bigr]dB_t.
\]
Under standard Lipschitz and linear-growth assumptions on \(f\) and \(G\) (Assumptions 1–2), the SDE admits a unique strong solution. The zero solution \(\varepsilon_t\equiv0\) is always a fixed point, but its stability is governed by the diffusion: the noise term contracts the expected squared perturbation \(\mathbb{E}[\|\varepsilon_t\|^2]\) when the diffusion coefficient is sufficiently large relative to the Lipschitz constant of \(f\). Consequently, small input perturbations (adversarial or random) do not grow unboundedly, yielding provable robustness improvements over the pure Neural ODE.

### Practical Benefits & Empirical Evidence
- **Generalization**: On CIFAR-10 the Neural SDE lifts test accuracy from 81.63 % (Neural ODE) to 84.55 % while keeping the same architecture.
- **Adversarial & non-adversarial robustness**: The stochastic trajectories average out adversarial directions; the paper reports consistent gains on STL-10 and Tiny-ImageNet under both \(\ell_2\)-bounded attacks and common corruptions.
- **Training**: Gradients are obtained via a stochastic-control adjoint method (distinct from the Neural ODE adjoint), enabling scalable back-propagation through the SDE.

### Summary
By embedding a learnable diffusion process \(G\,dB_t\) into the continuous-depth dynamics, Neural SDE converts the deterministic, potentially unstable Neural ODE flow into a regularized stochastic process whose sample paths remain bounded and whose perturbation dynamics are provably contractive. This directly transplants the beneficial effects of discrete noise-injection regularizers (dropout, Gaussian noise) into the continuous-depth regime.

## Certified Robustness to Adversarial Examples with Differential Privacy


---

arxiv_id: 1802.03471

version: 4

summary: Adversarial examples that fool machine learning models, particularly deep neural networks, have been a topic of intense research interest, with attacks and defenses being developed in a tight back-and-forth. Most past defenses are best effort and have been shown to be vulnerable to sophisticated attacks. Recently a set of certified defenses have been introduced, which provide guarantees of robustness to norm-bounded attacks, but they either do not scale to large datasets or are limited in the types of models they can support. This paper presents the first certified defense that both scales to large networks and datasets (such as Google's Inception network for ImageNet) and applies broadly to arbitrary model types. Our defense, called PixelDP, is based on a novel connection between robustness against adversarial examples and differential privacy, a cryptographically-inspired formalism, that provides a rigorous, generic, and flexible foundation for defense.

arxiv_id: 1812.00174

version: 1

summary: During the last few years, significant attention has been paid to the stochastic training of artificial neural networks, which is known as an effective regularization approach that helps improve the generalization capability of trained models. In this work, the method of modified equations is applied to show that the residual network and its variants with noise injection can be regarded as weak approximations of stochastic differential equations. Such observations enable us to bridge the stochastic training processes with the optimal control of backward Kolmogorov's equations. This not only offers a novel perspective on the effects of regularization from the loss landscape viewpoint but also sheds light on the design of more reliable and efficient stochastic training strategies. As an example, we propose a new way to utilize Bernoulli dropout within the plain residual network architecture and conduct experiments on a real-world image classification task to substantiate our theoretical findings.
